strengths: The authors present a learning effort framework over a number of problem settings to analyze optimal strategies for learning. Having an understanding and intuition about this can help our current deep learning design problems learn better.
The document motivates the problem well, emphasizing the importance of the work.
The arguments made by the work are linked to cognitive science and neuroscience, which can be used to get inspiration from when designing our current models.
The work conducts experiments over multiple paradigms, including meta-learning & continual learning.
By suitable choice of the control signal, one can model MAML, Bilevel Programming, task switch, and other techniques.
The experimental section is vast, well-described, and explained.
The paper is technically sound and presents a great exposition that helps the reader better understand the ideas in the paper.
The experiments are backed by an extensive appendix that clarifies details.
The writing style of the paper is excellent and the authors supplement their exposition with helpful explanations and figures (e.g., Fig. 1).
The proposed framework appears as a nice approach to reason about meta-algorithmic choices in the cognitive sciences and machine learning.
The authors derive a general framework and apply it to a range of experiments which seem to be well fleshed out.
I appreciate that the authors study an analytically tractable variant (linear networks) and derive results that seem to be consistent with the cognitive control literature.
I consider theoretical studies of the proposed kind interesting and relevant in their own right.
weaknesses: As pointed out by the authors themselves, a limitation is the assumption of linear models. Since the motivation behind the current work is to provide ways in improving the current neural networks, more analysis on non-linear systems is needed. Although very large neural networks are hard to analyze, simpler variations could be considered for non-linear settings to make this direction even more interesting. Specifically, the analysis could benefit from exploring how the control signals behave when the underlying system has non-linear activation functions and how this impacts the optimal learning effort.

Optimization is a big challenge in neural networks. An analysis focused on the effect of different optimization techniques might be helpful when extending the work on non-linear settings, which is currently being analyzed in only simpler artificial settings. For example, the paper could investigate how the learning effort framework interacts with optimizers like Adam or SGD with momentum, and whether the optimal control signals differ significantly from the linear case. This could also include an analysis of how different learning rates affect the optimal control policy.

A number of other biases exist in the cognitive literature, eg having modular systems in which different modules do different tasks, or learn them over multiple tasks. Analyzing this explicitly can be an interesting addition to the work. For instance, the framework could be extended to explore how control signals should be allocated when learning multiple tasks with shared and task-specific modules, and how this relates to the concept of transfer learning.
Figure 1 could be made a bit larger for better readability.

A simple two-layer linear neural network is used, so it may not account for all the effects during training, and the results may not translate to more complex NNs. Specifically, the non-linearities present in typical neural networks, such as ReLU or sigmoid activations, are absent, which drastically simplifies the optimization landscape. This simplification may lead to control policies that are optimal in the linear case but perform poorly when applied to non-linear networks. The framework's reliance on linear dynamics might also fail to capture phenomena like vanishing or exploding gradients, which are common in deep non-linear networks.

It's likely one will need to find a solution for every novel considered intervention. The analytical solutions derived for specific control signals may not generalize to new types of interventions, requiring a complete re-derivation of the learning dynamics and control optimization. This could become computationally expensive and limit the framework's scalability for exploring a wide range of meta-learning techniques. For example, if one wants to explore a new type of regularization, a new set of differential equations would need to be derived and solved.

I don’t think all interventions can be modeled within this framework, even when restricted to the context of two-layer linear neural networks. For example, interventions that involve non-local operations or those that depend on the entire history of the learning process may not be easily captured by the proposed framework. The framework's reliance on differential equations might struggle to model interventions that are discrete or involve complex dependencies on past states. This limitation could hinder the framework's ability to simulate certain meta-learning algorithms that rely on such interventions.
The main limitation of the paper is as the authors mention, based on the linear models they use. This limits applicability.
Another limitation is the lack of comparison against other meta-learning instances, where the evaluation could compare computational time.
I doubt that the results have any practical relevance for the design of modern machine learning/meta-learning algorithms.
The experiments are conducted on deep linear networks, which, while analytically tractable, are far removed from the non-linear architectures typically used in practice.

The control signals explored, such as parameter initialization and learning rate schedules, are already well-studied in the context of non-linear networks, and it is unclear if the optimal control signals found in the linear setting would generalize to more complex models.
The optimization of control signals is performed using gradient-based methods, which might be computationally expensive for high-dimensional control spaces, limiting the scalability of the approach.
